title: House of Wax
full_review:
There is at least 20 seconds of quality moviemaking in the otherwise repellent screamfest "House of Wax" (Warner Bros.). Unfortunately for the film's first-time director, Jaume Collet-Serra, those fleeting frames belong to a clip from Robert Aldrich's 1962 "Whatever Happened to Baby Jane?"

Billed as a "re-imagining" of the 1953 horror classic starring Vincent Price, this uninspired exercise in stomach-churning gore involves a group of college students (including Chad Michael Murray and Paris Hilton) who, while on a road trip to a big football game, find themselves stranded in a backwater quasi-ghost town somewhere between Gainesville, Fla., and Baton Rouge, La.

The creepy town's only attraction is the eponymous museum, made completely of wax, whose deranged curators -- a pair of homicidal twins (both played by Brian Van Holt) -- are intent on turning their unsuspecting victims into wax figures that are a little too lifelike for comfort. One of the twins was horribly disfigured when they were surgically separated at birth, resulting in a serious case of sibling rivalry (thus the "Baby Jane" reference).

Good-looking actors. Maniacs with knives. Vats of boiling hot wax. You fill in the blanks.

The plot is formulaic and as for the performances let's just say that better line-readings could be delivered by Madame Tussaud's waxen mannequins. Not that it matters much since "House of Wax" quickly melts into a bloody mess of slasher cliches and sadism, which, like last year's "Texas Chainsaw" remake, packages human debasement as popcorn fare, including an eye-averting scene of brutality involving a baseball bat and another where Hilton is harpooned through the forehead with a jagged metal rod.

The film's tagline is "Prey. Slay. Display" -- to which should be added "Stay Away!"

The film has gratuitous gruesome violence and gore, torture images, some sexual situations and humor, including a striptease and suggested oral sex, a scene of smoking and drinking, as well as recurring rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
